To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the relationship between shell-growth rates of A. islandiaca and environmental variables is complex and depends on the oceanographic setting of the habitat.
the correlation between shell-growth and SST in A. islandica is not stable over time and that the correlation between the shell growth of contemporaneous specimens is not stable over space.

(1) the relationship between shell thickness and SST in A. islandica in the Northeast Iceland area is highly variable over time and (2) this relationship depends on the oceanographic conditions prevailing during the time of growth.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reconstruction of the past climate from the shells of bivalve molluscs.
the development of a high-resolution and absolutely dated, annually resolved, multi-proxy climate archive from the North Atlantic Ocean.

the reconstruction of sea surface temperatures (SSTs) in the North Atlantic region during the last two centuries, using annually banded shells of the long-lived bivalve Arctica islandica from the surface waters off Iceland.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the correlation of shell growth of Arctica islandica with environmental variables is not only species- and habitat-specific, but also depends on the time period under consideration.

A. islandica is a good indicator of SST in the Northeast Atlantic Ocean, but only under the influence of one of the major surface currents, the Irminger Current and East Iceland Current, respectively, and not under their alternating influence.
SST is a major control on the shell growth of A.islandica in surface waters of Iceland but only if the habitat is influenced by the Irminger Current.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a statistically robust 178-year long composite chronology based on 16 A. islandica specimens from unpolluted shallow waters of Northeast-Iceland.
we have demonstrated that the growth of Arctica in Iceland is highly sensitive to the local SST and food availability.
the growth rates of A. islandca were higher during warmer and wetter years and that the growth rates were higher in years when the Irminger Current was stronger.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the growth of A. Islandica is not a reliable indicator of SST, and that it is important to take into account the oceanography of the area in which the bivalve lives.
A. islandica may not be suitable as an environmental indicator for the entire period covered by our chronology (1835–2013).
the relationship between shell-growth of Arctica islandia and environmental variables is complex, and that the relationship depends on oceanographic conditions.
